items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: I remember Kid Thomas would take a break, eat a sandwich.

ctx.x: Yeah, but not necessarily. Sometimes, maybe before the union, they might have even taken longer breaks at times. I mean, it depends on what would go on. I mean, but on the other hand, they were used to longer hours. I mean, they might start at 8 o'clock in the evening and play until 4 o'clock in the morning, even. And as far as long hours going, when you hear about these taxi dance halls, where they, you know, a dime a dance or a nickel a dance, they might have been in the old days, where they can hardly put…
You would remember more clearly than I, but for example, at Speck's Moulin Rouge, I remember Kid Thomas would take a break, eat a sandwich. Now, what time was that?

items.title: "Kid Thomas" Valentine Interview, 1969-01-27
items.q: Well, I made with Mr. Bill Russell.

ctx.x: No. Well, progressive, I don't like progressive. And they rock and roll. You best, I tell it, I tell you, one music I like the best, it's western, you know, like that, I prefer that kind of music. But they have nice, you know, they have nice numbers, you know. Because I feel, I feel, I used to feel a lot of western songs, when I was playing for dancers, you know. So, boy, they, you know, they came in. I don't like that, I don't understand it, that's why.
Well, tell me about your first recording session that you ever made. Well, I made with Mr. Bill Russell.
Yeah, that's the first one I made. That's the deal.

items.title: Betty Lee Hanson, Joe James, George Lewis, Joe Lewis, Joe Butler, Kid Thomas Valentine, Bill Russell, Allan…
items.q: even Kid Thomas, who's playing across the street, other people have used the same expression

ctx.x: Well, it is dying out, though, isn't it?

In that respect, it is. Since the jukeboxes, I don't know what it would be, whether it's the radio or jukeboxes or phonograph records or just what exactly killed it, but, well, even Kid Thomas, who's playing across the street, other people have used the same expression, exactly the same expression, that the city's like a cemetery, like a graveyard today, compared to how lively it was, say, 30 to 50 years ago that they remember.
Well, then maybe radio had a direct influence in cutting down some of it.
